item.title: AI without the Illusion of Intelligence: A Format Shift
item.description:
Why large language models are better understood not as an independent "artificial mind," but as a new class of human Information Tools. We too quickly agreed on what the two letters AI stand for. "Artificial Intelligence" has long been perceived not just as a historical term, but as a near-literal description of a new entity. From this name has grown the entire modern drama of human-machine relations: does AI think, does it understand us, will it become smarter than humans, whom will it replace, and when will it start making decisions independently? But perhaps the error occurs before all these questions—in the name itself. The term "artificial intelligence" preemptively suggests accepting the main assumption: we are dealing with a form of intelligence. After this, we inevitably begin to compare it with human intelligence. Meanwhile, large language models can be viewed in a different frame of reference—not as an emerging artificial subject, but as a human information tool, and then the familiar abbreviation takes on a different meaning: AI—Information Tool. Read more

item.title: Customer Requirements for LLM/AI Firewall
item.description:
Corporate AI is no longer a pilot project in a single department. Requests to models come from IDEs, internal assistants, agent loops, and "shadow" employee chats. The attack surface looks different from a classic perimeter: prompt injection, PII leakage to an external model, uncontrolled token consumption, an AI agent calling a tool without authorization. This article analyzes a real requirements matrix for an LLM/AI Firewall. The goal is not a feature catalog, but a map of what the Customer considers mandatory, and how these requirements translate into a control architecture where trust boundaries, cost, regulation, and manageability are important. Over the past year, large enterprise companies' requirements for generative AI protection have changed significantly. Initially, it was a short list of tasks for a "ChatGPT proxy." Now it's a multi-page matrix with over 500 formalized requirements: standard tasks first, then requirements for AI agents, MCP, 152-FZ, model supply chains, etc. This is no longer a request for a filter. It's a request for a control loop. Read more

item.title: MWS AI Agents Platform Review: A Platform for Creating AI Agents
item.description:
Almost everyone who has built an AI agent for business has gone through the same process: a quick prototype, a successful demo, and then months of work to add logging, monitoring, prompt versioning, access control, and deployment. Usually, I write about scientific articles on LLMs and AI in general. This time, the genre is different: I'll talk about MWS AI Agents Platform, a platform that handles the boilerplate needed to turn LLMs and theory from articles into working projects. The platform has been in production since the end of last year, but I'm only getting around to reviewing it now, after seven releases. I'll break down how it's structured, what you can build with it, and where its limitations lie. Read on

item.description:
It so happened that I completely missed agent systems. I decided that it was worth filling this gap and catching up. My enthusiasm cooled down a bit during the work process, and I want to share the first results. item.title: Why an AI Agent is Not a Digital Employee
item.description:
An AI agent already performs part of the work previously done by humans. But this doesn't make it a digital employee. A person joins an organization not only with knowledge but also with professional norms, an understanding of the context of rules, and boundaries that don't need to be explicitly defined. An agent lacks these supports by default. The article explores how to replace them and why agent platforms and frameworks are insufficient. They provide management mechanisms, but the organization will have to extract their content from its own practices, employee knowledge, and formulate it explicitly. At the end, there are eight questions to answer before launching an agent, rather than after the first incident.

item.title: I Made an AI Editor for Habr — and Had to Figure Out if I Was Building an AI Slop Factory
item.description:
I wanted to automate technical article writing and ended up creating StoryOps: a system that reads an author's past publications, researches a repository, fact-checks, and analyzes current platform materials. Then the uncomfortable question arose: how is this different from another AI slop factory? I tried to figure it out with numbers: how much AI content is already online, why there's so much of it on TikTok and YouTube, why audiences reject it, how platforms are dealing with it, and where the line is between AI as a tool and a garbage conveyor belt. item.title: Google Gave AI Agents a Face. Gemini 3.8 Live Creates Talking Avatars in Real Time
item.description:
Google introduced Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar. The model accepts voice, image, video, and text, and responds through an animated character with lip-sync, facial expressions, and voice. This is not a separate talking-head generator attached to a chatbot. The avatar is built directly into the conversational model and can see the interlocutor, listen to them, respond, and access external services during the conversation. Read more

item.title: Qwen3.8–27B on two RTX 3060 12GB: How I overclocked OpenCode from ~9 to ~40 tokens/s with 128K context
item.description:
Is it possible to turn two RTX 3060 12GB cards on an old Z97 platform into a decent local backend for OpenCode? I started with 9 tokens/s on a long context and ended up with about 40 tokens/s in a real agent session with over 100K context, without reducing the model size or sacrificing 128K context. This article covers tensor split without CUDA P2P, Q8 KV-cache, integrated MTP, n-max tuning, failed experiments with NCCL and shared buffers, real long-context tests, and quality checks on coding tasks. Read on

item.title: Evaluating AI Agents: 7 Mistakes That Make Tests Lie
item.description:
A green status on eval tests doesn't guarantee an AI agent is working correctly: it might give the right answer but perform incorrect actions or none at all. This article examines seven common mistakes in evaluating AI agents and shows which approaches help measure the system's real quality. Let's break down the errors.

item.title: Brain Machine Learning
item.description:
A dog training collar on your forearm, a wire to your laptop's COM port, a Portuguese phrase in your headphones. Make a typo, and you get a shock. I do machine learning, and one day I asked a question that would make any teacher squirm: what's the fundamental difference between how humans learn and how models learn? Then, for two years, I tested the answer on the most complex subject of all—my own brain. It's half past one in the morning. A dog training collar is strapped to my left forearm—the one with the metal contacts. A wire runs from it to the COM port of an old laptop. On the screen is a Portuguese phrase; I hear it in my headphones and have to type it blind. My finger hovers over the key. I know: make a typo, and I'll get a shock. Not a strong one. Just enough. Why an adult man, an engineer, a father of three, sits up at night and electrocutes himself for typos in Portuguese is a long story. It began with desperation, went through several wild experiments, and ended with a working system that my whole family is now learning with. I'll tell you the whole story. And let me preface this by saying, so the collar doesn't seem like a mere gimmick for a dramatic opening: without this madness, none of the rest would have happened. It was this that showed me why the signal stops working altogether—and from that grew everything that truly keeps me and my family at the table today. So, we'll come back to it, more than once. Read on.

item.title: 1700 lines of JS and not a single video file: how an AI agent makes a movie on Canvas and renders it to MP4
item.description:
This minute-long film contains no images, video files, or samples. Fire, engraving, a 3D sphere, a pixel game, and music are drawn and synthesized by a single HTML file of 1700 lines, written by an AI agent. Without rules, the same agent produces a dull screensaver: blue background, neon, everything moves linearly. I'll break down what changes this: a frame as a pure function draw(ctx, t), rendering to MP4 without a single stutter, and an agent that self-checks the film by timecodes. Read more
